Q: What's the best way to manage Java versions in 2026? A:

Disclosure: I wrote jolta, the tool described below.

If you want the nvm/pyenv experience for Java — fast, installs versions for you, switches on cd, keeps JAVA_HOME right — that's exactly what jolta is built for.

Single static binary, written in Rust with no runtime dependencies. Nothing to source, no shell framework, no plugins to install.

Setup

brew install OneAppPlatform/tap/jolta
jolta setup

setup installs the shims, puts them on PATH, and adds the JAVA_HOME hook to your shell profile. Open a new shell and you're done.

Per project

cd ~/work/service-a && jolta pin 21    # writes .java-version
cd ~/work/service-b && jolta pin 17

That's the whole workflow. cd between them and java, javac, mvn, gradle and JAVA_HOME all follow automatically. No activate, no use, no re-running anything in each new terminal.

$ cd ~/work/service-a && java -version
openjdk version "21.0.11" 2026-04-15
$ cd ~/work/service-b && java -version
openjdk version "17.0.19" 2026-04-15

The parts that map to your list

It installs JDKs for you. jolta pin 25 on a machine that doesn't have 25 fetches it. So does running java under a pin you don't have — the download happens on first use, not on cd, so entering a directory never blocks on the network.

jolta install 21           # explicit
jolta install corretto@21  # a specific distribution
jolta install lts          # whatever LTS currently means
jolta list                 # what you have, and which is active
jolta current              # what applies here, and why

JAVA_HOME, not just PATH. This is the one that bites people: Maven and Gradle read JAVA_HOME, so a switcher that only manipulates PATH leaves you with a java on the command line that disagrees with your build. jolta keeps both in sync.

Nearest pin wins. .java-version is resolved by walking up from your current directory, so a monorepo can pin per module:

repo/.java-version           -> 21
repo/svc-legacy/.java-version -> 17

cd repo/svc-legacy gets 17;
everything else in the repo gets 21.

Already have .sdkmanrc files? jolta reads them. You don't have to convert your repos or get the whole team to switch first.

macOS, Linux and Windows. Windows setup writes the user PATH in the registry and installs the JAVA_HOME hook into your PowerShell profiles. (Windows install is a zip download and .\jolta.exe setup for now — a winget package is submitted and awaiting review.)

The IDE half

Your shell being right doesn't make IntelliJ right, and that gap is where most of the remaining pain lives. The IntelliJ plugin reads the same .java-version and sets the Project SDK, the Gradle JVM and the Maven importer JDK from it — no configuration.

It also follows along live: run jolta pin 25 in a terminal, or pull a teammate's commit that changes the pin, and the IDE switches within seconds. No restart, no re-import. Java run configurations get JAVA_HOME and PATH pointed at the pinned JDK too, so a test that shells out to a build agrees with the editor.

Uninstalling

Worth knowing before you commit to anything:

jolta implode

Q: application insights vs elastic (ELK) A:

We have to find new ways of Observability using App insights or ELK , paired with MCP servers and Claude.ai for inferencing and prompts
I have written a post about it
https://azurebysagar.wordpress.com/2026/08/09/new-ways-of-observability-using-claude-ai-mcp-and-correlation-id/

  1. You can use Azure app insight or ELK
  2. Write MCP servers or use existing once
  3. Integrate that with claude.ai etc
  4. Write corelation logging or make use trace id from app insights
  5. Identify entire stack trace and root cause whenever you see any exception using few prompts

IMO , we should be more talking about Observability than just creating dashboards , bebcasue In case of production issues , identifying issues faster is more important than which tool we are using!

Q: Need to change the colour of line numbers in neovim A:

The tokyonight setup function accepts options as documented in the README file. Among the options, you can pass a function named on_highlights to override default values. Because each style has its own dedicated file (night, moon, storm, and day), I think it's best that the style is also specified. This solution is provided for the moon style, but it works for other styles as well. It is tested on version 0.12.4 and works for versions >= 0.8.0 according to the documentation:

require('tokyonight').setup({
  style = 'moon',
  on_highlights = function(hl, c)
    -- Controls color of LineNr for the line that the cursor is on.
    -- The default value is "#3b4261".
    hl.LineNr = {
      fg = c.dark5
    }
    -- Controls color of LineNr for all lines above the line the cursor is on.
    -- The default value is "#3b4261".
    hl.LineNrAbove = {
      fg = c.dark5
    }
    -- Controls color of LineNr for all lines below the line the cursor is on.
    -- The default value is "#3b4261".
    hl.LineNrBelow = {
      fg = c.dark5
    }
  end
})

I have put part of the explanation in the comments inside the snippet. Tokyo Night provides colors (the second argument of the on_highlights function) that you can use for convenience. The hex value corresponding to each color is automatically adjusted to suit each colorscheme, by tokyonight. I used the one I thought was suitable, but you can go ahead with your own options. You can find what you can use by consulting the referenced files, based on the style you want to use. You can also specify the color yourself (fg = "#587539" for instance). For an even more visible line number you might consider using c.fg or c.fg_dark instead.

Alternatives (and their advantages and disadvantages):

There are other ways to achieve something similar, each with drawbacks compared to the presented solution.

  1. By specifying on_colors in the options (as explained in this answer): This approach affects every highlight group that uses that color, not just the intended ones. You can test this by overriding dark5 as demonstrated below:
require('tokyonight').setup({
  style = 'moon',
  on_highlights = function(hl, c)
    hl.LineNr = { fg = c.dark5 }
    hl.LineNrAbove = { fg = c.dark5 }
    hl.LineNrBelow = { fg = c.dark5 }
  end,
  on_colors = function(colors)
    colors.dark5 = '#f52a65' -- red
  end
})

I personally found no advantage in using this approach.

  1. By manually overriding using neovim API (as explained in this answer):

Advantages: This works regardless of the colorscheme or plugins, as long as you place the function after where the colorscheme is loaded. It also allows you to override any highlight group without being restricted to the plugin's API.

Disadvantages: This approach hardcodes raw hex values, so your line number colors will not adapt if you switch between tokyonight styles. More broadly, this method encourages a pattern of having the system fight itself: you load a theme and then manually override its output. In a configuration where the colorscheme is already fixed to tokyonight, this adds unnecessary bloat and is less maintainable than using the theme's own, designed API.

Q: What is the difference between a keyword and a clause in SQL? A:

KEYWORD :-> Everything that belongs to SQL is a keyword, something with a particular definition(example:-> SELECT, WHERE, FROM, etc).

CLAUSES :-> Meaningful logic(changeable) created using keywords of SQL, but can't be executed individually, needs more specific clauses attached together(example:-> SELECT name, FROM employees, WHERE salary>180000, etc).

STATEMENT :-> An SQL Query formed using combining specific Clauses together making a meaningful thing overall that can be executed(example:-> SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary>180000, etc).
